items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models are increasingly deployed in iterative self-refinement workflows, wherein a model repeatedly revises its own outputs in pursuit of improved quality. Despite the growing prevalence of such systems, the long-term dynamics of repeated self-improvement remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether iterative refinement exhibits convergence toward stable semantic states. Experiments were conducted using FLAN-T5-Small, FLAN-T5-Base, and TinyLlama across multiple optimization objectives and application domains. Semantic trajectories were quantified using sentenceembedding similarity and modelled through exponential decay functions. Across architectures, objectives, and domains, iterative refinement consistently exhibited high-quality exponential convergence, indicating progressive stabilization of semantic representations. No statistically significant differences were observed across optimization objectives or application domains, suggesting a surprising degree of invariance in the refinement process. To account for this phenomenon, the concept of semantic fixed points is introduced, defined as stable response states toward which iterative refinement converges. A complementary theoretical framework is proposed in which self-refinement acts as an implicit semantic optimization process traversing an underlying energy landscape and converging toward locally stable attractors. Under this interpretation, the observed exponential convergence emerges naturally from fixed-point dynamics within semantic space. These findings provide empirical evidence that iterative language model self-refinement exhibits stable convergence behaviour across diverse settings and motivate future investigations into the mathematical structure of semantic attractors, convergence dynamics, and autonomous self-improving AI systems.</jats:p>
title: Toward a Theory of Semantic Fixed Points: Evidence from Iterative Language Model Self-Refinement

<jats:p>Modern distributed software systems fail in ways that static recovery policies cannot anticipate and that human
operators cannot address at production speed. Rule-based autonomic systems are constrained to pre-defined failure modes, while
learning-driven agents risk uncontrolled behavior during exploration in live environments. This paper presents Project Phoenix,
an autonomous self-healing framework that addresses this challenge through a closed-loop architecture integrating Tree-ofThoughts (ToT) deliberation for structured pre-execution multi-path recovery planning with Self-Refine iterative correction for
post-execution policy refinement. The framework spans continuous health monitoring, probabilistic failure detection, multistrategy autonomous decision-making, coordinated multi-agent recovery execution, iterative self-correction, and reinforcementlearning-based policy adaptation. Internal validation across 3,416 automated test cases demonstrated implementation
consistency across all tested scenario families; external benchmarking against independent workloads is identified as future
work.</jats:p>
title: Project Phoenix: Autonomous Self-Healing via Tree-of-Thoughts Deliberation and Self-Refine Iterative Correction

items.abstract: <jats:p>In industry NLP application, our dataset by prompting large language models (LLMs) has a certain number of noise data. We present a simple method to find the noise data and remove them. We retain the data that contains certain common tokens between the LLMs data and the prediction results of a generative model trained on the LLMs data. We remove the data that does not contain certain common tokens between the LLMs data and the prediction results of a generative model trained on the LLMs data. We adopt T5-Base as our generative model. The experiment result shows our method is highly effective and does not require any manual annotation. For industry deep learning application, our method improves the NLP tasks accuracy from 88% to 98% under human evaluation, meanwhile the LLMs data source is sufficiently abundant.</jats:p>
title: Self-Refine Learning For Cleaning LLMs Data
